source.title: Gadam: Combining Adaptivity with Iterate Averaging Gives Greater Generalisation
source.authors: Diego Granziol; Xingchen Wan; Stephen J. Roberts

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, though its title differs from the provided TITLE and venue metadata; the text identifies it as “Iterate Averaging in the Quest for Best Test Error.”
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own optimizer and iterate-averaging comparisons on natural-label datasets, plus measured train/test performance and sharpness properties. These are conceptual tests of parts of the optimizer/generalization and measured-property versions, with different interventions and measures from the original studies.
record.gate_note: No random-label memorization test, width sweep, convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison, batch-size comparison, dropout intervention, magnitude-aware sharpness measure, or memorized-example removal is reported. The study's own results on natural-label classification bear on V4 and V6's weight-decay comparison only insofar as it measures the optimizer/generalization association; its sharpness table bears on V7's generalization-gap property. Cited prior-work results are not rows. Figure-only learning curves and parameter-count trends are not transcribed as precise values.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares adaptive optimizers with SGD using held-out accuracy and perplexity, testing V4. A training-to-test gap is not required by V4. Its weight-decay experiments do not test dropout in V6, and its unscaled Hessian metrics do not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance in V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors propose a Gaussian-process explanation for averaging benefits and report strong results for Adam-based Gadam/GadamX with suitable regularization. They also report near-monotonic late-training held-out improvements and preliminary evidence of reduced tuning needs. Their appendix finds that averaging lowers curvature relative to its iterates but that these Hessian metrics do not clearly track generalization. Ordinary Gadam does not beat SGD in every setting, and its strongest ImageNet results require additional recipe changes.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains natural-label image classifiers with iterate averaging and optimizer/weight-decay variants; it does not reproduce the source methods for the listed claim versions. Its comparisons do not isolate the adaptive optimizer effect consistently, including differing terminal learning rates in the sharpness table.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports sensitivity to iterate-averaging frequency, weight decay, batch normalization, learning rate, and averaging starting point. The appendix sharpness comparison varies terminal learning rate and optimizer.

fits_no_version.finding: Averaging generally lowers Hessian curvature relative to its iterates, but curvature does not consistently order held-out performance. In Table 13, Gadam at terminal rate 3E−4 achieves 71.55% test accuracy versus SGD's 71.64%, despite substantially larger Hessian metrics.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unscaled local Hessian curvature need not reliably rank test accuracy across optimizer and learning-rate choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Iterate averaging improves held-out performance relative to its base optimizer, with gains depending on learning rate, weight decay, batch normalization and averaging choices.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Iterate averaging with an appropriate training recipe can improve generalization.

record.peer_reviewed: Journal of Machine Learning Research 1 (2021) 1-48; submitted 07/21, published TBD
record.problems: The property measurements use one architecture and dataset in the sharpness table; the authors state they did not tune optimizers rigorously for that exposition. The table changes terminal learning rates across optimizers, complicating comparisons. No error bars are reported for these sharpness measurements.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible numeric results are left out. Main benchmark results compare optimizers with iterate averaging, but do not measure a training-to-test error gap for the versions and are not included as rows. Figures 1–12, 14 and tables 1–12 contain other optimizer/averaging metrics that do not directly measure the claim versions' named behaviors or properties.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label held-out generalization.
Widening past zero training error; parameter-count trends in averaging benefits are a different comparison.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.

An experiment restricting tuning exclusively to learning rates and schedules; switching from Adam to SGD; a systematic broad-tuning comparison across all optimizers. Image experiments also tune weight decay, and some proposed methods alter averaging and adaptivity.
Large-versus-small batch performance under matched epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
All dropout claims. Weight-decay variation alone does not test dropout or joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its correlation with generalization gaps, and its ranking against norm and margin measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

missing.what: Restore direct base-optimizer held-out comparisons: Tables 1, 2 and 4 compare SGD with AdamW and partially adaptive methods across CIFAR and ImageNet-32. These are eligible V4 results despite the record declaring them excluded; V4 does not require a measured training-to-test gap.
missing.locator: Sections 6–6.1; Tables 1, 2 and 4; Table 9 duplicates the CIFAR-10 results

missing.what: Record ImageNet optimizer comparisons and their recipe conditions: Table 3's ResNet-50/101 results; ResNet-18 AdamW 69.92% versus SGD 69.72%; ordinary Gadam ResNet-50 75.52% and learning-rate-adjusted Gadam 76.53%. Distinguish the large numerical-stability constant used for Table 3's Gadam from ordinary Gadam.

Record PTB optimizer and schedule comparisons: ASGD test perplexity 61.98±0.19, Adam 63.16±0.24, Gadam 58.77±0.08, GadamX 60.45±0.04; scheduled Adam 61.51 and NT-ASGD 64.73. These expose the schedule-dependent ordering omitted from the record.
missing.locator: Section 8, Table 5; Appendix D.2, Tables 10–11; Appendix C.2

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for any listed version. The existing rows mostly capture averaging and unscaled curvature, while the direct V4 comparisons were incorrectly excluded. Missing entries identify that eligibility error despite the blanket rows_left_out declaration. The appendix prose's 14-fold spectral-norm comparison conflicts with Table 13: 43/4.40 is approximately 9.8; its Frobenius and trace ratios are approximately 92 and 23.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width beyond interpolation threshold and test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Broad optimizer benchmark tuning, word-level language-model comparisons where Adam can outperform, and switching from Adam to SGD.
Large versus small batch under fixed epoch budgets and workload-dependent batch-size effects.
Dropout intervention and its effects by training-set size; joint dropout and weight-decay removal with augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation sharpness, the specified norm/margin comparisons, and CIFAR-10/SVHN without augmentation.
Removing highly memorized examples and comparing against random removals.

relationships.condition: Base AdamW versus SGD on the tested deeper image classifiers, with the study's learning-rate, schedule and weight-decay choices
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict; eligible comparison rows are missing. AdamW trails SGD on ResNeXt/CIFAR-100 (80.16 versus 81.47), WRN/ImageNet-32 (55.51 versus 61.33), and ResNet-50/101 ImageNet (74.04/74.48 versus 75.63/77.37). This supports the held-out disadvantage in these recipes, without establishing equal training performance.
relationships.display_finding: Reported accuracy favored SGD over base AdamW across the specified deeper classifiers, but these comparisons remain unverified and equal training performance was unestablished.

relationships.condition: ImageNet ResNet-18 with AdamW versus SGD
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict; Section 7 reports AdamW at 69.92% versus SGD at 69.72%. The observed ordering reverses on this architecture, qualifying the scope of the disadvantage; uncertainty is not reported.
relationships.display_finding: Reported AdamW accuracy of 69.92% versus SGD's 69.72% remains unverified and lacks uncertainty estimates.

relationships.condition: Adaptive methods with iterate averaging, appropriate regularization, and sometimes reduced adaptivity
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict; Tables 1–4 show recipe-dependent recovery. Gadam exceeds SGD on VGG-16/CIFAR-100 (75.73 versus 74.15) but remains below it on ImageNet-32 (60.50 versus 61.33); GadamX reaches 63.04 there. Table 3's strongest ImageNet settings additionally change numerical stability or adaptivity. These results qualify the optimizer disadvantage under adapted recipes.
relationships.display_finding: Reported recovery with Gadam and GadamX remains unverified and varies with workload, regularization, numerical stability, and adaptivity.

relationships.condition: PTB word-level LSTM: constant versus scheduled Adam, compared with averaged SGD
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict; Tables 5 and 11 report test perplexity 63.16 for constant-schedule Adam versus 61.98 for ASGD, but 61.51 for scheduled Adam; NT-ASGD gives 64.73. The optimizer ordering depends on scheduling and the averaging trigger within the 200-epoch budget.
relationships.display_finding: Reported perplexity comparisons remain unverified. Which optimizer performs better depends on Adam's schedule and when averaging begins in SGD.
